In the Supreme Court of the United States
NATIONAL REPUBLICAN CONGRESSIONAL COMMITTEE 
AND NATIONAL REPUBLICAN SENATORIAL COMMITTEE,
APPLICANTS,
v.
SHERROD BROWN, JON OSSOFF, ROY COOPER,
AND KRISTEN MCDONALD RIVET,
RESPONDENTS.
EMERGENCY APPLICATION FOR STAY AND ADMINISTRATIVE STAY
PENDING PETITION FOR WRIT OF CERTIORARI
To the Honorable John G. Roberts, Jr.,
Chief Justice of the United States and
Circuit Justice for the Fourth Circuit
October 8, 2026
THOMAS R. MCCARTHY

DAVID L. ROSENTHAL

- ii -
PARTIES TO THE PROCEEDING AND RELATED PROCEEDINGS
The parties to the proceeding below are as follows: 
Applicants are the National Republican Congressional Committee and the 
National Republican Senatorial Committee. Applicants were intervenor-respondents in the court of appeals proceedings.
Respondents are Sherrod Brown, Jon Ossoff, Roy Cooper, and Kristen McDonald Rivet. Respondents were applicants in the agency proceedings and petitioners in 
the court of appeals proceedings.
The Federal Communications Commission is also a Respondent. It was a respondent in the agency proceedings and in the court of appeals proceedings.
The related proceedings below are:
1. In re: Brown, 26-2230 (4th Cir.) – Judgment entered October 7, 2026;
Applicants’ stay motion filed October 7, 2026, denied October 7, 2026;
FCC stay motion filed October 7, 2026;
2. National Republican Congressional Committee v. Brown, No. 26A274, 
(U.S.) – Stay entered September 4, 2026;
3. Brown v. Federal Communications Commission, No. 26-1785 (4th Cir.) 
– Judgment entered August 25, 2026;
4. In the Matter of Entitlement to Lowest Unit Charge for Legally Qualified Candidates for Federal Office and All Authorized Committees, DA 
26-300 (Federal Communications Commission) – pending

- 1 -
TO THE HONORABLE JOHN G. ROBERTS, JR., CHIEF JUSTICE OF THE UNITED
STATES AND CIRCUIT JUSTICE FOR THE FOURTH CIRCUIT:
Just one month ago, this Court stayed a Fourth Circuit order interfering with
the Federal Communication Commission’s lowest-unit-charge rules “in the critical 
weeks leading up to the midterms.” NRCC v. Brown (Brown I), No. 26A274, 609 U.S. 
__ (Sept. 4, 2026) (slip op. at 3). Intent on its aim to throw out longstanding rules
before the midterms, the same Fourth Circuit panel has since awarded mandamus to 
the same group of federal candidates seeking review of the same FCC public notice. 
This time, the panel acted in the middle of an open comment cycle. As Judge Wilkinson put it, “[t]he grant of a writ of mandamus is a direct affront to the Supreme 
Court’s stay order in this case.” App.40 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting). 
If the case for a stay was strong the first time around, it’s open and shut now.
In Brown I, this Court held that “the Fourth Circuit likely lacked jurisdiction” to review a staff-level public notice regarding broadcasting rates for political committees, 
since the Federal Communications Commission was still considering the “application 
for review.” Brown I, 609 U.S. __, slip op. at 3. The Commission is still considering 
that application. In fact, the Commission opened an expedited comment period, partly 
in response to the Fourth Circuit and a dissenting commissioner “suggesting that 
releasing any decision on the Application for Review without some sort of public process would amount to a legal error.”1 The Commission requested comment in part on 
1 See Public Notice DA 26-982, Media Bureau Seeks Comment on Application for Review of Public Notice Pertaining to Lowest Unit Charge Requirements, (FCC Sept. 15, 
2026), perma.cc/4DZP-XQCN.

- 2 -
the appropriateness of changes this late in the election cycle, given this Court’s finding that political parties would be irreparably harmed by late-breaking rule changes
affecting their speech. Public Notice DA 26-982, supra note 1, at 2.
Again, the Fourth Circuit short-circuited agency review. It should have followed this Court’s stay in Brown I, which “inform[s] how a court should exercise its 
equitable discretion in like cases.” Trump v. Boyle, 145 S. Ct. 2653, 2654 (2025). Instead, it “ignored the Supreme Court’s concern and unraveled its work” by granting 
the extraordinary relief of mandamus. App.40 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting). Worse yet,
this order comes even later than Brown I and inflicts greater injury closer to the election. To vindicate its Brown I order, the Court should again stay the Fourth Circuit’s 
judgment. 
Even if the Court were to look at the remaining mandamus factors, the candidates don’t come close to showing they are entitled to the “‘drastic and extraordinary’ 
remedy ‘reserved for really extraordinary causes.’” Cheney v. U.S. Dist. Ct. for D.C., 
542 U.S. 367, 380 (2004). The Fourth Circuit lacks jurisdiction to review the Commission’s public notice top to bottom, so mandamus cannot be in “aid of [its] respective 
jurisdictio[n].” 28 U.S.C. §1651(a). Even if the Fourth Circuit did (or would) have jurisdiction to review the public notice, the Commission hasn’t “failed to take a discrete 
agency action that it is required to take.” Norton v. S. Utah Wilderness All., 542 U.S. 
55, 64 (2004). It need not rule on the application for review by any particular deadline, 
let alone bypass an ongoing comment period to cater to the political whims of the

- 3 -
Candidates. At a minimum, those are not “crystal-clear legal dut[ies]” that can justify 
mandamus. In re Nat’l Nurses United, 47 F.4th 746, 752 (D.C. Cir. 2022).
The Fourth Circuit ordered the Commission “to resolve by 12:00 noon on Friday, October 9, 2026, the Federal Candidates’ Application for FCC Review.” App.35
(majority op.). Given that impending order, Applicants request a stay of the 
Fourth Circuit’s judgment and mandate. They also request an immediate 
administrative stay before the Fourth Circuit’s impending deadline of 12:00 
PM this Friday, October 9.
STATEMENT OF THE CASE
The Court has seen this case before. The legal and factual background hasn’t 
changed since Brown I. Only the procedural posture is different: rather than rule on 
the merits, the Fourth Circuit granted mandamus.
A. The Federal Election Campaign Act amended the Communications Act of 
1934, requiring broadcasters to offer “a legally qualified candidate” for a federal office 
“and any authorized committee of the candidate” the “lowest unit charge of the station for the same class and amount of time for the same period” in the runup to an 
election. 47 U.S.C. §315(b)(1)-(2). Candidate “use of any broadcasting station” triggers 
the “lowest unit charge” entitlement, known as the “LUC Rule.” Id. §315(b)(1). Both 
the FCC and the broadcasting industry have long taken the position that coordinated 
ad buys and joint-fundraising-committee ad buys for candidate use receive the favorable LUC rate. And that’s the way it’s always been done.
The Candidates sought to upset that status quo as election day draws near. 
They challenged a public notice issued by the Commission’s Media Bureau in March

- 4 -
that “remind[ed] broadcasters and the public about the FCC’s lowest unit charge 
(LUC) requirements.” Guidance on Entitlement to Lowest Unit Charge for Legally 
Qualified Candidates for Fed. Off. & All Authorized Committees, No. DA 26-300, 2026 
WL 1013722, at *1 (FCC Mar. 30, 2026). The notice reiterated that the lowest unit 
rate applies to both “authorized committees, including authorized committees that 
engage in joint fundraising with legally qualified candidates for federal office,” and 
to “advertisements that qualify as coordinated expenditures of political parties and 
legally qualified candidates for federal office.” Id. The Candidates filed an application 
for review, asking the full Commission to revisit and set aside that guidance. The 
Commission is still considering that application. 
On June 22, while their application was pending before the Commission, the 
Candidates petitioned for review in the Fourth Circuit. The Republican Committees
intervened to prevent last-minute changes to the lowest-unit-charge rules. On August 
25, a split panel granted the petition, denied the Commission’s motion to dismiss, and 
set aside “the Public Notice issued by the FCC’s Media Bureau.” Brown v. FCC 
(Brown I), __F.4th__, 2026 WL 2493115, at *12 (4th Cir. Aug. 25, 2026). Judge Wilkinson dissented. The panel denied the Republican Committees’ stay motion and sua 
sponte expedited issuance of the mandate to take effect that day. Again, Judge Wilkinson dissented.
The Republican Committees applied for a stay in this Court, which granted the 
application on September 4. The Court held that “[b]ecause the candidates’ applica-

- 5 -
tion for review was pending when they filed their petition for review, the Fourth Circuit likely lacked statutory jurisdiction to address their challenge.” Brown I, 609 U.S.
__, slip op. at 3. It also held that the Republican Committees “demonstrated that they 
will likely suffer irreparable harm absent a stay” because the Fourth Circuit’s order 
was “hampering their efforts to reach the electorate in the critical weeks leading up 
to the midterms,” which “implicates their First Amendment rights to speak and coordinate their political activities freely.” Id. (citing NRSC v. FEC, 146 S. Ct. 2404, 2414-
16 (2026)). The Court thus granted the application, stayed the Fourth Circuit’s judgment, and recalled the mandate. Id. at 4.
B. Undeterred, the Candidates sought to end run this Court’s stay order. Four 
days after the Court issued that order, the Candidates returned to the Fourth Circuit.
This time, they petitioned for a writ of mandamus, seeking an order “requiring the 
Federal Communications Commission to issue a decision on [their] Application for 
Review by September 18.” App.81. The case was assigned to the same Fourth Circuit 
panel that handled Brown I. On the Candidates’ motion, the panel expedited briefing, 
ordering the Commission to answer the petition in six days. App.55.
Again, Judge Wilkinson dissented. He wrote that “[a]ny attempt to proceed at 
this late date to introduce multiple advertising rates and new campaign finance 
ground rules in the middle of the election season is a direct affront to the Supreme 
Court and its stay order.” App.56 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting from order expediting
briefing). He added that this Court’s “stay order stressed the importance of not keeping matters in a continually unsettled state in the ‘critical weeks leading up to the

- 6 -
midterms.’” App.56 (quoting Brown I, 609 U.S. __, slip op. at 3). The Fourth Circuit 
granted Republican Committees’ motion to intervene, and the parties briefed the expedited mandamus petition.
Meanwhile, “the FCC went to work.” App.42 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting). The 
Commission opened an expedited comment period on the Candidates’ application for 
review. See Public Notice DA 26-982, supra note 1. That comment period addressed 
a dissenting commissioner’s criticism for releasing the public notice “without seeking 
comment,” which she claimed deviated from the “normal process.” Statement of 
Comm’r Anna M. Gomez, In re: Entitlement to Lowest Unit Charge, No. DA 26-851, 
2026 WL 2583279, at *1 (FCC Aug. 25, 2026). The Fourth Circuit likewise thought it 
relevant in Brown I that the Commission did not “seek responses from impacted parties, or engage in fact finding, or secure supplemental briefing, or solicit public comment, or schedule or conduct an oral argument.” __F.4th, 2026 WL 2493115, at *6. 
And the Commission set that comment cycle on a far “shorter timeline” than is typical. See Public Notice DA 26-982, supra, at 2.
In light of the comment period, the Fourth Circuit deferred action on the mandamus petition “until at least October 1, 2026.” App.51. Again, Judge Wilkinson dissented. He would have “den[ied] the petition for a writ of mandamus” outright since 
deferred action “keep[s] matters churning, in direct contradiction of the Supreme 
Court’s instruction that matters should be left in a stable state ‘in the critical weeks 
leading up to the midterms.’” App.53 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting from order deferring 
action) (quoting Brown I, 609 U.S. __, slip op. at 3). Judge Wilkinson criticized the

- 7 -
majority for “emphasiz[ing] Congress’s aspirational timelines after consistently casting shade on the agency’s authority to act at all.” 354 (citation omitted).
The expedited comment period remains ongoing because of a related application for review. Like the Candidates here, the Television Bureau of Advertising asked
the Media Bureau to reconsider its public notice on the lowest-unit-charge rule. See 
In re Entitlement to Lowest Unit Charge for Legally Qualified Candidates for Federal 
Office and All Authorized Committees, DA 26-851, 2026 WL 2427163 (FCC Aug. 13, 
2026). The Media Bureau first dismissed the petition for lack of jurisdiction, since the 
public notice is not a “final agency action.” Id. at *1. After this Court’s stay order in 
Brown I, the Television Bureau sought the full Commission’s review of the Media 
Bureau’s dismissal and of the underlying public notice. App.46. The Television Bureau’s application raised “issues that substantially overlap with petitioners’ challenges, and also a separate First Amendment challenge.” App.46. In part because “the 
Communications Act makes the disposition of ‘all applications for review filed in any 
case’ a precondition to judicial review,” the Commission opened a comment period on 
the Television Bureau’s application. App.47 (quoting 47 U.S.C. §155(c)(7)). And although “the FCC generally provides the public with at least 30 days for comment,” the 
Commission determined “that a shorter timeline is more appropriate.” App.49. Comments in the Television Bureau matter are due October 12; replies are due October 
19. App.48.

- 8 -
In the midst of the ongoing comment period, the Fourth Circuit granted mandamus. Displeased even with the expedited process, the panel thought the Commission should move faster. So it ordered the Commission to “resolve by 12:00 noon on 
Friday, October 9, 2026, the Federal Candidates’ Application for FCC Review.” 
App.34. The Fourth Circuit first found that because this Court’s stay order “has kept 
the Public Notice in effect,” the “Candidates have no other adequate remedy through 
which they could obtain relief.” App.14. It then conjured up a finding that the Candidates “have a clear right to relief” and the Commission “has a clear duty to act” because federal law “requires that the Commission ‘shall pass upon’ every application 
for review.” App.31 (citing 47 U.S.C. §155(c)(4)). The Fourth Circuit rejected the Commission’s argument that it should not disturb the rules this close to the election, finding the argument “irreconcilable with the reality that the Public Notice’s stated purpose was to address the impending election.” App.32. Finally, the Fourth Circuit 
found that “the procedural posture” weighs in favor of mandamus, since the underlying question about the lowest-unit-charge rule is “a matter of pure statutory interpretation.” App.33. The panel never addressed the Republican Committees’ arguments that they would be irreparably harmed by mandamus. 
Again, Judge Wilkinson dissented. He criticized the majority for flouting “the 
Supreme Court’s stay order in this case.” App.40 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting). He highlighted the “intangible damage” that mandamus would work to the existing and future contracts in this election cycle. App.40. He disputed the majority’s characterization of agency delay, stating that “this is more a case of judicial meddling than agency

- 9 -
neglect.” App.41. And “even in the face of far greater delays and far more egregious 
circumstances,” the majority cited “no cases it claims are analogous to this one.”
App.41-42. As for the Commission’s ongoing comment period, the majority “tacitly 
endors[ed]” the procedure, “since the majority complained, in its earlier opinion, that 
the FCC had not yet called for comments.” App.42. So, as Judge Wilkinson put it, 
“[t]he FCC’s only ‘extraordinary’ demerit is a lack of mind-reading talent. It is to be 
punished for sloth when it supposedly lacked jurisdiction, and then condemned for 
industry when it obeyed our instructions.” App.43. Finally, Judge Wilkinson criticized the majority for “tinkering” with the FCC’s lowest-unit-charge rules “after they 
go into effect.” App.43. The panel’s order “palpably disregards the Supreme Court’s 
stay order,” thus “disrupting settled campaign finance rules in the hot breath of an 
impending election.” App.43.
The Republican Committees and the Commission moved for emergency stays
in the Fourth Circuit on October 7. App.2, 9. The Fourth Circuit has not yet ruled on 
the Commissions’ motion, but it denied the Republican Committees’ motion on the 
same day. App.1. For the sixth time, Judge Wilkinson dissented.
ARGUMENT
This Court will stay a circuit court’s order if there is “(1) a reasonable probability that four Justices will consider the issue sufficiently meritorious to grant certiorari; (2) a fair prospect that a majority of the Court will vote to reverse the judgment 
below; and (3) a likelihood that irreparable harm will result from the denial of a stay.” 
Hollingsworth v. Perry, 558 U.S. 183, 190 (2010) (per curiam). “In close cases the 
Circuit Justice or the Court will balance the equities and weigh the relative harms to

- 10 -
the applicant and to the respondent.” Id. Applicants satisfied those standards the 
first time, and this Court ordered a stay. By granting mandamus in the face of that 
stay order, the panel majority invited this Court to “Say It Twice.” App.40 (Wilkinson, 
J., dissenting). If anything, it’s easier for Applicants to satisfy the stay factors the 
second time around.
I. There is a reasonable probability that four Justices would vote to 
grant review and a fair prospect that this Court would reverse.
Mandamus “is a ‘drastic and extraordinary’ remedy ‘reserved for really extraordinary causes.’” Cheney, 542 U.S. at 380 (citation omitted). The Candidates’
budget woes are not “really extraordinary.” Id. Indeed, the only extraordinary thing 
about this case is the panel majority’s lack of “respect for the Supreme Court” and its 
stay order in Brown I. App.43 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting). The Court is likely to grant 
certiorari and reverse for at least three reasons.
A. The Fourth Circuit’s “grant of a writ of mandamus is a direct 
affront to the Supreme Court’s stay order in this case.” 
When the Candidates sought rushed relief in Brown I, this Court put on the 
brakes for this election cycle. As Judge Wilkinson flagged at the outset of the mandamus proceedings, “[a]ny attempt to proceed at this late date to introduce multiple 
advertising rates and new campaign finance ground rules in the middle of the election 
season is a direct affront to the Supreme Court and its stay order.” App.56 (Wilkinson, 
J., dissenting from order expediting briefing). This Court’s stay “inform[s] how a court 
should exercise its equitable discretion in like cases.” Boyle, 145 S. Ct. at 2654. And 
there’s no doubt that these cases are alike. The same panel handled the same matter 
brought by the same parties litigating the same injuries. That the Candidates seek

- 11 -
even more extraordinary relief at an even later date are differences—they’re just differences that make the Fourth Circuit’s tinkering “still worse.” App.43 (Wilkinson, 
J., dissenting). 
The Fourth Circuit never acknowledged that this Court already balanced the 
equities in this case. To the contrary, it found that the Candidates “have no other 
adequate remedy … because, by staying on jurisdictional grounds this Court’s mandate in Brown I, which set aside and held for naught the Public Notice, the Supreme 
Court has kept the Public Notice in effect.” App.30 (majority op.) (emphasis added). 
But that’s just a concession that this Court balanced the harms the first time around, 
and held that the Republican Committees’ irreparable injuries outweighed the Candidates’ alleged injuries. Those injuries are not the same. The Republican Committees suffer “irreparable harm” from an order that would lead broadcasting stations to 
cancel existing and future contracts in the midst of the election. Brown I, 609 U.S. __, 
slip op. at 3-4. By contrast, the Candidates claim an injury from their competitors
having equal access to favorable broadcasting rates, and thus assert a right to interfere with those contracts. This Court didn’t credit that injury the first time around. 
See generally id. And if this Court didn’t explicitly “‘balance the equities and weigh 
the relative harms,’” it’s only because Brown I wasn’t a “close cas[e].” Id. at 3. Either 
way, the Fourth Circuit erred in exercising its “equitable discretion.” Boyle, 145 S. 
Ct. at 2654.

- 12 -
B. The Fourth Circuit cannot order mandamus to preserve nonexistent jurisdiction.
The All Writs Act gives federal courts authority to “issue all writs necessary or 
appropriate in aid of their respective jurisdictions and agreeable to the usages and 
principles of law.” 28 U.S.C. §1651(a). “As this statutory language makes clear, the 
Act is not itself a grant of jurisdiction.” In re Tennant, 359 F.3d 523, 527 (D.C. Cir. 
2004) (Roberts, J.). “Instead, it authorizes the issuance of a writ of mandamus in aid 
of jurisdiction [the] court already has or will have as a result of issuing the writ.” 
Nat’l Nurses, 47 F.4th at 752 (citing Tennant, 359 F.3d at 527). But here, mandamus 
neither preserves existing jurisdiction nor protects future jurisdiction.
Start with existing jurisdiction, since this Court already addressed it. The 
Court concluded in Brown I that “the Fourth Circuit likely lacked jurisdiction to issue” its vacatur order. 609 U.S. __, slip op. at 3. Courts cannot grant mandamus “in 
aid of jurisdiction” they don’t have. Nat’l Nurses, 47 F.4th at 752. If “the court does 
not and would not have jurisdiction to review the agency action sought by petitioners, 
it cannot bootstrap jurisdiction via the All Writs Act.” Id. This Court’s holding in 
Brown I that “the Fourth Circuit likely lacked jurisdiction,” 609 U.S. __, slip op. at 3, 
means the Fourth Circuit can’t mandamus itself into jurisdiction in Brown II. 
Nor would mandamus protect the Fourth Circuit’s future jurisdiction. The 
Fourth Circuit never even claimed it could. Indeed, back in August, one of the panel 
members remarked that it “elude[d] him” how “mandamus could be a solution … in
the months before an election.” Brown I, 2026 WL 2493115, at *13 n.1 (Wynn, J.,
concurring). Mandamus is appropriate only to compel agency acts that “if and when

- 13 -
taken, would be within [the court’s] appellate jurisdiction.” Tennant, 359 F.3d at 530. 
But as the Republican Committees and the Solicitor General explained the first time 
around,2 the public notice is not a final agency action “from which legal consequences 
will flow.” Bennett v. Spear, 520 U.S. 154, 177-78 (1997) (cleaned up). The D.C. Circuit 
has thus held that an FCC bureau order issued under delegated authority “is not an 
order of the Commission,” and “without a final order from the Commission,” courts 
lack jurisdiction. NTCH, Inc. v. FCC, 877 F.3d 408, 409-10 (D.C. Cir. 2017). Neither 
the staff-level public notice—nor any future order disposing of the application for review—determine “rights or obligations” or have “legal consequences.” Bennett, 520 
U.S. at 177-78 (cleaned up). At most, they “advise the public of [the Media Bureau’s] 
construction of the [Act].” Perez v. Mortgage Bankers Ass’n, 575 U.S. 92, 97 (2015).
They do not have “the force and effect of law.” Id. That the “‘cause already instituted’
before the agency” is not judicially reviewable means that mandamus “cannot be justified as ‘in aid of’ [the court’s] prospective appellate jurisdiction over the FCC under 
the All Writs Act.” Tennant, 359 F.3d at 530 (quoting Marbury v. Madison, 5 U.S. (1 
Cranch) 137, 175-76 (1803)). In short, the Fourth Circuit lacks jurisdiction to review 
the public notice at all, so speeding up the Commission’s review cannot be appropriate 
grounds for mandamus.
2 See Appl. for Stay at 9-11, Brown I, No. 26A274 (U.S. Aug. 28, 2026); Br. for the 
United States at 13-16, Brown I, No. 26A274 (U.S. Aug. 31, 2026).

- 14 -
C. The Candidates do not have a “clear and indisputable right” to 
bypass an ongoing comment period. 
Only “if the court has jurisdiction,” can it “consider whether the agency has a 
crystal-clear legal duty to act.” Nat’l Nurses, 47 F.4th at 752. The Court can stop 
there, and stay the mandamus order. But even if the Fourth Circuit had jurisdiction, 
the writ “remains ‘reserved only for the most transparent violations of a clear duty to 
act.’” Id. (quoting In re Core Commc’ns, 531 F.3d 849, 855 (D.C. Cir. 2008)). The 
Fourth Circuit began its analysis with the premise that the Commission “‘shall pass 
upon’ every application for review.” App.31. On that premise, it ordered the Commission “to resolve by 12:00 noon on Friday, October 9, 2026, the Federal Candidates’ 
Application for FCC Review.” App.34. Missing from that logical leap is the other necessary premise: that the Commission has a “clear duty to act” on the application for 
review by October 9, in the midst of an ongoing comment period in the middle of an 
election. Nat’l Nurses, 47 F.4th at 752.
The Fourth Circuit purported to find a deadline in an inapplicable and aspirational time period. It claimed that “the Commission is obligated to enter orders that 
are ‘necessary or appropriate to expedite the prompt and orderly conduct of the business of the Commission with the objective of rendering a final decision … within three 
months’ from when an application for review is filed.” App.31 (quoting 47 U.S.C. 
§155(d)). But the majority omitted the key language from its quote: that three-month 
objective applies to “the date of filing in all original application, renewal, and transfer 
cases in which it will not be necessary to hold a hearing.” 47 U.S.C. §155(d). And an 
“original application” (§155(d)) is not an “application for review” (§155(c)). Rather, an

- 15 -
“original application” refers to the Commission’s core activities: “Applications for TV 
stations” and other broadcasting licenses. E.g., 47 C.F.R. §73.3572(a). Those are the 
sorts of applications that can request “renewal” of a license or “transfer” control of a 
station. E.g., Application for Cable Television Relay Service Station License, Form 
327, FCC (Nov. 2020), perma.cc/8RC7-XTNP. So in context, §155(d)’s three-month 
timeline for “original application, renewal, and transfer cases” refers to those applications that apply for, renew, or transfer licenses—not applications for review.
Even if §155(d) referred to applications for review, the three-month timeline is 
“aspirational,” not mandatory. App.53 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting from order deferring 
action). The majority attempted to spin the statute by insisting the Commission is 
“obligated” to observe that timeline. App.31. But adding “obligated” before Congress’s 
words can’t transform the statute into what the majority would prefer it to say. Congress assigned an “objective of rendering a final decision” within three months after 
an application is filed. 47 U.S.C. §155(d). That’s discretion, not a “clear duty to act.”
Lovitky v. Trump, 949 F.3d 753, 760 (D.C. Cir. 2020). Even if the command were 
stronger, the Commission has no clear duty to act on the Candidates’ preferred schedule, especially when doing so would bypass a comment period at least “tacitly endors[ed]” by the Fourth Circuit, App.42 (Wilkinson, J., dissenting), and inflict “irreparable harm” on parties to the case in the midst of election season, Brown I, 609 U.S.
__, slip op. at 3.
Agency inaction is eligible for mandamus relief when the agency has “failed to 
take a discrete agency action that it is required to take.” Norton, 542 U.S. at 64. But

- 16 -
here, the Commission has not “failed” to act, let alone failed to take the “discrete” 
action of abiding by the Candidates’ preferred timeline. Id. To the contrary, “[t]he 
Commission is actively reviewing” the comments submitted by the Candidates and 
numerous other groups, App.46, and doing so on a far “shorter timeline” than is typical, App.49. The Commission can hardly be faulted for taking seriously suggestions 
that the absence of “some sort of public process would amount to a legal error.” Public 
Notice DA 26-982, supra note 1, at 2. And the Candidates do not have a “‘clear and 
indisputable’” right to bypass the normal agency process. See Kerr v. U.S. Dist. Ct. for 
N. Dist. of Cal., 426 U.S. 394, 403 (1976).
Even if the Commission weren’t still in a comment period, the Candidates don’t 
have a clear right to an agency order on their preferred timeline—particularly where
that timeline would impose “irreparable harm” on Applicants. Brown I, 609 U.S. __, 
slip op. at 3. Mandamus petitions routinely fail for the mistake the Fourth Circuit 
made here by “conflat[ing]” an agency’s discretionary duty to take a specific action 
with a “non-discretionary duty” to act in general. Nat’l Nurses, 47 F.4th at 756. Without a “specific, unequivocal command” that the Commission must resolve applications 
by a specific deadline, the pace of the Commission’s decisionmaking “is left to the 
agency’s discretion.” See Norton, 542 U.S. at 63-65 (cleaned up). So even if the Fourth 
Circuit could order the Commission to “pass upon” the application, it could not compel 
it to do so by a particular date. See id. at 65 (“[W]hen an agency is compelled by law 
to act within a certain time period, but the manner of its action is left to the agency’s 
discretion, a court can compel the agency to act, but has no power to specify what the

- 17 -
action must be.”). Courts construe the agency’s duty narrowly, asking “‘whether the 
agency has a crystal-clear legal duty to act.’” In re W. Coal Traffic League, 108 F.4th 
905, 909 (D.C. Cir. 2024) (citation omitted). But there’s no “crystal-clear legal duty” 
to bypass the comment period and resolve the Candidates’ application on their preferred timeline.
Framing the issue as one of “pure statutory interpretation” doesn’t relieve the 
Fourth Circuit of these rules. Cf. App.33. When this Court overturned Chevron, it told

Bureau has extended to political parties favorable campaign advertising rates to which 
under law only the candidates themselves are statutorily entitled. And the Commission has 
since delayed agency review in an obvious effort to preclude judicial review prior to the 
November 3 election day. If allowed to continue dragging its feet, the FCC will have

principle of judicial review. See Marbury v. Madison, 1 Cranch 137, 177 (1803) (Marshall,

qualified candidate for any public office in connection with his campaign” must not exceed

period.” See 47 U.S.C. § 315(b)(1)(A). Pursuant to the plain statutory language, it has

that requires broadcasters to extend the LUC to political parties engaged in coordinated 
expenditures with candidates and to joint fundraising committees with political-party and 
other non-candidate members. Although the Public Notice purports to merely restate 
previous Media Bureau guidance concerning LUC eligibility, it identifies no previous 
Media Bureau guidance specifying that non-persons and non-candidates — political parties

I would deny the motion to expedite and I would deny any issuance of a writ

Congressional Committee v. Brown, No. 26A274, 609 U.S. __ (2026) (slip op. at 3);

INTRODUCTION
Two weeks ago, this Court held in Brown v. FCC that the Federal 
Communications Commission’s Media Bureau violated the Communications Act 
when it issued a Public Notice on March 30, 2026, that instructed broadcasters to 
offer “lowest unit charge” advertising rates to political parties and joint fundraising 
committees, because the Act reserves those rates for candidates only. Brown v. FCC 
(“Brown I”), No. 26-1785, 2026 WL 2493115 (4th Cir. Aug. 25, 2026), stay granted 
sub nom. NRCC v. Brown, No. 26A274, 2026 WL 2618462 (U.S. Sep. 4, 2026) (per 
curiam). On Friday, the Supreme Court stayed that decision on procedural grounds 
only, ruling that the Court likely lacks jurisdiction to review the Public Notice while 
Petitioners’ Application for Review of the Public Notice remains pending before the 
FCC. See NRCC, 2026 WL 2618462. In doing so, however, the Supreme Court did 
not question Brown I’s merits conclusion that the Public Notice is unlawful, and it 
recognized that the Public Notice is not an ordinary economic regulation, but rather 
one that implicates “efforts to reach the electorate in the critical weeks leading up to 
the midterms.” Id. at *2.

to address the Supreme Court’s jurisdictional concern and enable a decisive ruling 
on the validity of the Public Notice before it is too late to matter. There is no

I. Statutory and Regulatory Framework
A. The Communications Act requires broadcasters to charge 
candidates “lowest unit charge” for advertising before elections.
Section 315(b)(1) of the Communications Act of 1934 entitles “legally 
qualified candidate[s] for any public office” who “use . . . any broadcasting station” 
shortly before their elections to do so at “the lowest unit charge of the station for the 
same class and amount of time for the same period.” 47 U.S.C. § 315(b)(1) (“the 
LUC requirement”). This valuable entitlement takes effect 45 days before the

candidate’s primary election and 60 days before the general election. Id.
§ 315(b)(1)(A). Its present text was enacted as part of the Federal Election Campaign 
Act of 1971 (FECA), which comprehensively regulates federal campaign finances. 
See Hernstadt v. FCC, 677 F.2d 893, 897 (D.C. Cir. 1980).
FECA requires all federal candidates to designate a “principal campaign 
committee” to accept contributions and make expenditures on the candidate’s behalf. 
52 U.S.C. § 30102(e)(1). Everyone agrees that stations must offer lowest unit charge 
for advertisements purchased by those principal campaign committees on behalf of 
the “legally qualified candidate” they support. This Petition concerns whether 
stations must also offer lowest unit charge to advertisements purchased by two other 
categories of committees that are further removed from the candidates themselves: 
party committees engaged in coordinated expenditures under 52 U.S.C. § 30116(d), 
and joint fundraising committees established by candidates and non-candidates 
“solely for the purpose of joint fundraising,” id. § 30102(e)(3)(A)(ii). 
Party Committee Coordinated Expenditures. FECA sharply limits the size 
of “contributions” that may be made to federal political committees, including 
candidate committees. See 52 U.S.C. § 30116(a). To prevent donors from evading 
those limits by directly paying vendors on a candidate’s behalf, FECA generally 
treats as contributions, subject to those same limits, expenditures that are “made by 
any person in cooperation, consultation, or concert, with, or at the request or

§ 30116(a)(7)(B)(i). But as the Supreme Court held a few months ago, political party 
committees are constitutionally entitled to make unlimited “coordinated” 
expenditures, which, the Court explained, “are the party’s expenditures on, for 
example, advertisements produced or distributed in consultation with a candidate’s 
campaign.” NRSC v. FEC, 146 S. Ct. 2404, 2413 (2026). 
Joint Fundraising Committees. In addition to establishing a principal 
campaign committee, FECA allows federal candidates to “designate a political 
committee established solely for the purpose of joint fundraising by such candidates 
as an [additional] authorized committee.” 52 U.S.C. § 30102(e)(3)(A)(ii); 11 C.F.R. 
§ 102.17(a)(1)–(2). Such committees are known as “joint fundraising committees” 
or “JFCs.” A JFC’s only permissible purpose is to “collect contributions, pay 
fundraising costs from gross proceeds and from funds advanced by participants, and 
disburse net proceeds to each participant.” 11 C.F.R. § 102.17(b)(1); see 52 U.S.C. 
§ 30102(e)(3)(A)(ii). FEC regulations require JFC participants to split expenses for 
fundraising in proportion to their share of the proceeds. 11 C.F.R. § 102.17(c)(7).
In recent election cycles, Republican candidates have formed JFCs with noncandidate committees as advertising vehicles. These JFCs are structured to ensure
